newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid agencies have access to refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies have access to refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Aid agencies in this rebel-held city in eastern Zaire had full access on Saturday to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees camped along a rail track after a six-month nightmare of fleeing the country's civil war.

The reality on the ground south of Kisangani contradicted international appeals to the rebels to allow aid workers to help the sick and exhausted refugees who are dying at the rate of about 120 a day.
The local head of the U.N. refugee agency, Filippo Grandi, was puzzled on Friday night by the clamour abroad for access.
"We need to have access, which we have. I didn't see a single (rebel) soldier today.
"The second issue is to stabilise the refugees, which is happening. They have not moved for the last 72 hours," Grandi, the UNHCR coordinator for eastern Zaire, said in Kisangani.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said on Saturday 151 refugees had died on Friday among 80,000 south of Kisangani and a total of 2,397 cases of severe malnutrition had been registered.
"Malnutrition at this point is the biggest enemy," he said.
The European Union's special envoy, Aldo Aiello, arrived on Saturday in Kisangani, captured from President Mobutu Sese Seko's collapsing army on March 15.

Aiello planned to visit the refugees as the senior official in Kisangani from the rebels' Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) called for the refugees to be repatriated as quickly as possible.

On Friday, as for the previous days, teams from U.N. and private agencies brought food, shelters and medical care to the refugees who have tramped up to 600 kms (400 miles) inland since the start of Laurent Kabila's rebellion last October.
"We are working day by day to provide basic needs," Karen Coyne of the charity Oxfam told reporters as her team put up a water purification system 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani.
About 80,000 of the refugees are now stationary at km 25 (mile 15) and further south at km 42 (mile 26).
About 20,000 others, with more groups straggling in from the thick jungle, are strung out along the 125-km (75-mile) rail line from Kisangani to Ubundu.
The Hutus, who include about 2,000 from Burundi, are the largest group of an estimated 300,000 refugees dotted around eastern Zaire, most in territory now controlled by the rebels.

The Ubundu track marks the end of the line for the refugees, the desperate rearguard of more than two million Rwandan Hutus who fled their country in July 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels now in government.

They fled with the former army and the Interahamwe militia which led the genocide of about 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda from April to June, 1994. The third anniversary of the start of the mass slaughter is on Sunday.
The others have returned to their homeland, either by choice or under duress, and now the group south of Kisangani say they want to do the same.
"I want to leave now, even tonight. Everyone will go back," said Therese Uwimana, a teacher aged 29 who fled southern Rwanda with her two children in 1994.
Aid agencies were unhappy when the authorities in Kisangani refused to allow the refugees into or near the city.

But the new governor, Yagi Sitolo, criticises the United Nations dragging its feet and assuming the Hutus, who include ex-Rwandan army soldiers, could be sheltered in or near the dilapidated and dirty northeast capital of about 500,000 people.
"We have just come through 30 years of dictatorship and yet they want to bring a mass of refugees to the gates of the city, causing problems of security, food, health and environment," he said.
The ADFL official in charge of refugees, Deo Senki Sibomana, said the rebels wanted them repatriated by road from Ubundu.

Aid workers are seriously contemplating one of the world's biggest refugee airlifts from Kisangani, flying the 100,000 Hutus back to Rwanda at a cost estimated by the UNHCR of $50 million or $500 per passenger for the 90-minute flight.
"Let them fix up the refugees, treat them and then move them to Ubundu. They can be trucked home from there," Senki said.
The road option via Ubundu is daunting as well, with rains approaching and sections likely to be impassable for trucks.
